---
title: "Weather normalisation, step by step"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
# Training and normalising take minutes at realistic budgets, so the chunks are
# shown but not run when the site is built. The Getting started vignette runs
# the same steps on a small subset.
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = FALSE)
```

`nm_do_all()` runs the whole normalisation in one call (see the
[README](https://github.com/apai-sys/normet-r#quick-start)). This article does
the same work one step at a time, so that each step can be inspected, tuned and
reused. The [Getting started](normet.html) vignette runs these steps on a
small subset of the data, with output.

The example uses the bundled `my1` dataset. It holds hourly NO2 at London
Marylebone Road (MY1) for January to August 2020, together with meteorology.

```{r}
library(normet)

covariates <- c("ws", "wd", "temp", "RH", "atmos_pres", "blh", "tcc", "tp", "ssrd")
predictors <- c(covariates, "date_unix", "day_julian", "weekday", "hour")
```

`covariates` are the weather variables. `predictors` adds the time features
that `nm_prepare_data()` computes from the `date` column.

## 1. Prepare the data

```{r}
df_prep <- nm_prepare_data(
  df             = my1,
  target         = "NO2",
  covariates     = covariates,   # weather only: time features are added here
  split_method   = "random",
  train_fraction = 0.75
)
```

The target column is renamed to `value` and a `set` column marks the training
and testing rows.

## 2. Train a model

```{r}
model <- nm_train_model(
  df           = df_prep,
  target       = "value",
  covariates   = predictors,
  backend      = "lightgbm",          # or "h2o": see the Backends article
  model_config = list(n_trials = 50, cv_folds = 5)
)

nm_modStats(df_prep, model)           # performance on the training and testing sets
```

`nm_build_model()` does steps 1 and 2 in one call and returns both `df_prep`
and `model`. Models can be saved with `nm_save_model()` and restored with
`nm_load_model()`.

## 3. Explain the model

```{r}
# Feature importance
nm_feature_importance(model)

# Partial dependence plots
pdp_data <- nm_pdp(df_prep, model, var_list = c("blh", "RH"))
nm_plot_pdp(pdp_data)
```

## 4. Normalise for weather

`nm_normalise()` repeatedly resamples the weather variables and averages the
model's predictions. The result is a "de-weathered" series, from which the
weather-driven variation has been removed.

```{r}
df_norm <- nm_normalise(
  df            = df_prep,
  model         = model,
  resample_vars = covariates,
  n_samples     = 600
)
nm_plot_normalise(df_norm)
```

Rather than guessing `n_samples`, `nm_normalise_auto()` draws resamples in
batches and stops once the whole series has converged:

```{r}
auto <- nm_normalise_auto(
  df            = df_prep,
  model         = model,
  resample_vars = covariates
)
cat("Samples used:", auto$best_n, "\n")
head(auto$res)   # date | observed | normalised
```

`nm_normalise_ext()` adds two options: it can restrict the resampling pool
(`conditional_on`) and return quantiles of each date's resampled distribution
(`return_quantiles`).

## 5. Rolling normalisation

For trend analysis, `nm_rolling()` normalises within a moving window and
produces one normalised value per window for each timestamp:

```{r}
df_rolling <- nm_rolling(
  df            = df_prep,
  target        = "value",
  model         = model,
  resample_vars = covariates,
  n_samples     = 300,
  window_days   = 14,
  rolling_every = 7
)
nm_plot_rolling(df_rolling, data = df_prep)
```
